messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rafael is a 62-year-old married Latino man who has spent most of his adult life as a dancer, and he still teaches and rehearses in a studio where bodies move close together and touch is part of the work. The collision happened late one evening as he was driving home after class. Another car ran a light and struck the driver’s side hard enough to spin his vehicle. What has stayed with him is not a clear story but fragments that come back with force: the explosive crash of metal, the shriek of brakes, a horn blaring somewhere too long, and the sensation that events had outrun his ability to act. When he tries to describe it, he stalls out and says it is “like noise and impact, not words.” In those moments of recall he feels a wave of shame that is hard for him to explain, as if there is something humiliating in having been so exposed and overpowered.

In the months after the crash, Rafael found that entering any room had become a quiet tactical exercise. At the studio, before he could focus on music or choreography, he was already noting the exits, the door to the hall, the back stairwell, who was standing where. If a student came up behind him and touched his shoulder unexpectedly, he jerked violently and felt a surge of alarm out of proportion to the moment. He was often flooded with fear, anger, and shame afterward. He had come to believe that bad things could happen without warning and that he was the kind of person they happened to. That sense of helplessness and character-based blame made every space feel less safe; scanning for ways out and bracing against sudden contact felt necessary, not excessive.

The heightened vigilance also seemed to sharpen the way the crash returned to him. When he was already on edge in rehearsal, a squeal from the sound system or the scrape of a chair could bring back the sound of the collision in his head with startling immediacy. The memory did not come as a coherent narrative but as auditory fragments and bodily shock, leaving him tense and ashamed before he had fully registered why. He noticed that the more keyed up he was—watching doors, flinching at touch, feeling his body ready for danger—the more easily these sensory pieces broke through.

Because those intrusions felt unbearable and almost impossible to speak about, Rafael began managing them the only ways he could think of. He tried hard not to think about the crash at all, cutting off conversations and mentally shoving images away the instant they began. At night he stayed up very late, lingering over television or sitting awake in the dark because sleep felt too unguarded and because closing his eyes made the sounds more likely to come. Sometimes, when the memory pressed in, he deliberately tried to blank out and “go somewhere else,” describing it as leaving his body just enough not to feel the full force of it. These strategies gave him brief relief, but they also seemed to leave the event even less put into words; what remained were the same raw sounds, the same unspeakable fragments, and the same shame each time they returned.

Over time, these habits changed how Rafael understood himself. Because he was avoiding the memory rather than making sense of it, he became more convinced that something in him had been permanently altered. He had come to believe he would never feel normal emotions again, only some mixture of fear, anger, and deadness. When he found himself staying up half the night or mentally disappearing in the middle of distress, he took this not as a sign of struggle but as evidence of damage: proof, in his mind, that he was weak, defective, the sort of man to whom terrible things happen and who cannot stop them. The very methods he used to get through the day deepened his bleak view of himself.

That view, in turn, kept the sense of threat close. If he was inherently vulnerable and the world fundamentally uncontrollable, then of course he needed to watch every doorway and keep his body ready. In class he has become more distant with students, stepping out of partnering demonstrations when possible and positioning himself near the studio exit. His wife has noticed he lingers awake long after she has gone to bed and seems elsewhere when she asks about the accident. Rafael finally sought help after startling so intensely when a younger dancer adjusted his arm from behind that he shouted and stopped rehearsal cold. What frightened him most was not only the reaction itself, but the conviction that this was now his permanent self: a man who cannot speak the worst thing that happened to him, cannot trust safety when it is present, and may never feel like himself again. He says he is coming now because he wants, more than anything, to know whether the crash still has to live in his body this way.
